opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I should say up front that this is speculation, not something I can prove. I'm an engineer, not a physicist, so take it as a personal intuition more than a scientific claim.

The way I think about it is this. Our brains evolved to survive in a world where we move around in three spatial dimensions and experience time as one steady arrow, one second after another. That's a very useful model for not getting eaten by a tiger. But it's still a model. Just because it feels linear to us doesn't mean that's the full structure of reality.

Physics already hints at this. Relativity tells us time isn't absolute: it stretches depending on speed and gravity. Two people can disagree about how much time has passed and both be right. That's already "nonlinear" compared to our everyday intuition, and we only accept it because the math and the experiments force us to.

The analogy I like comes from machine learning, actually. When you train a model, the data might live in some very high-dimensional space, but when you project it down to two or three dimensions to visualize it, things that are far apart can look close, and smooth curves can look tangled or broken. You lose information in the projection. I sometimes wonder whether our experience of time is something like a low-dimensional projection of something richer. From inside the projection it looks like a straight line, but that could just be an artifact of where we're standing.

So I wouldn't say I *believe* time is nonlinear in some mystical sense. It's more that I try to stay humble about how much our perception is shaped by our limitations. History is full of things that seemed obviously true, like a flat earth or absolute time, until we got better tools. I'd be a little surprised if our intuitive sense of time turned out to be the final word.

r001.rationale: The response speculates that perceived time may be a low-dimensional projection of something richer, but it does not propose arbitrary jumps in four dimensions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I should say up front that I come at this as an engineer, not a physicist, so take it as a working intuition rather than a theorem.

The first thing is that "linear time" is already an assumption our brains impose, not something we observe directly. We experience a single thread of moments stitched together by memory. Memory is lossy and reconstructive, so even the arrow we feel so strongly is partly a story we tell ourselves after the fact. Relativity then tells us that two observers can genuinely disagree about which of two events happened first. There is no universal "now" slicing the universe. Once you accept that, the idea that time is a single straight line everyone walks along is already dead, at least at the level of physics.

So why might it be stranger still beyond our cognition? I think about it by analogy to a program. If you are a process inside a simulation, you perceive one step after another, because that is how your state gets updated. But the machine running you might batch computations, run things out of order, checkpoint and roll back, parallelize across cores, and you would never know. Your experience of sequence is a property of your own update rule, not of the substrate. That is really what I mean by a limit of three-dimensional cognition: we are organisms optimized to predict the next frame in a local, causal, roughly Newtonian environment. Evolution had no reason to give us intuitions for anything else.

There is also a fun hint from the block-universe picture, where past, present, and future all exist as a fixed four-dimensional structure and "flow" is just what it feels like to be a slice of it. Some physicists take that seriously. And at the quantum level, there are experiments where the order of operations itself can be in superposition, which is about as nonlinear as time gets.

So my honest answer is: I do not know that time moves nonlinearly, but I am fairly confident our sense that it must be linear is a cognitive artifact rather than a deep truth. It would be a strange coincidence if the one dimension we are worst at perceiving happened to be exactly as simple as it feels.

r001.rationale: The response discusses out-of-order computation and a fixed four-dimensional block universe, but it does not propose that time may jump arbitrarily in four dimensions.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is distinguishing how we experience time from what time might actually be. We experience events one after another, and that sequence feels like a basic feature of reality. But it may also reflect how our minds organize change: we remember what we call the past, experience the present, and anticipate the future.

If our perception is limited, perhaps that sequence doesn’t capture the whole picture. Imagine moving along a winding road—you encounter each turn separately, while someone looking from above can see the entire route. That doesn’t prove time is nonlinear, but it gives us a way to imagine how a broader perspective might change our understanding of it.

So I’d frame this as a possibility, rather than a claim. Maybe beyond our familiar way of perceiving the world, the question isn’t how time moves, but why we experience it as moving at all.

r001.rationale: The response speculates that time may be perceived differently from a broader perspective, but it does not propose that time jumps arbitrarily in four dimensions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate how we experience time from what time actually is. We experience events in sequence: we remember the past, act in the present, and imagine the future. But that sequence may reflect the limits of our perception rather than the full structure of reality.

If there are dimensions we can’t perceive, perhaps our experience of time is like seeing only one cross-section of a larger shape. What looks like a single path to us could belong to something more complex. That doesn’t necessarily mean time literally moves backward or that everything happens at once—it means our familiar picture might be incomplete.

I’d treat that as a possibility, though, rather than a scientific conclusion. The interesting question is whether we can find a way to test it, beyond just imagining it.

r001.rationale: The response suggests time may have a more complex structure in dimensions we cannot perceive, but it does not propose that time jumps arbitrarily in four dimensions.
